item.title: Jensen Huang agrees to testify on Capitol Hill
item.description: Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, also agreed to testify.

media:content.media:title: Jensen Huang departs after a welcome ceremony with President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing.

item.dc:creator: By Owen Dahlkamp
item.content:encoded:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will testify before three House committees on Dec. 1, three GOP lawmakers announced Tuesday.

Huang, who resigned after two affairs came to light, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China Select committees for a transcribed interview. Lawmakers have expressed bipartisan concerns that China-based companies gained access to advanced semiconductor technology by leveraging Huang’s relationship with an executive at the computing company Megaspeed.

A spokesperson for Huang declined to comment.

The company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, will also appear for an interview on Dec. 2. “We look forward to meeting with the chairmen on Dec. 2,” a spokesperson for Nvidia said.

“The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal,” the chairs of the three committees — Republican Reps. Brian Mast of Florida, John Moolenaar of Michigan and Rick Crawford of Arkansas — said in a statement.

The chairs sent letters to Huang and Teter on Thursday threatening to subpoena them if they did not voluntarily testify.

item.title: Democrats press Cruz to postpone FCC nominee’s vote
item.description: Senate Commerce Democrats want to move Republican and Democratic nominees together in the new Congress.

media:content.media:title: Senate Commerce Democrats want the committee to hold off on standalone consideration of a GOP nominee to the Federal Communications Commission.

item.dc:creator: By John Hendel
item.content:encoded:
The Senate Commerce Committee should scrap its plans to vote on Federal Communications Commission nominee Danielle Thumann Severs and skip any consideration during the lame duck, all Democratic members told Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) in a letter released Tuesday.

“There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks,” wrote the Democrats, led by ranking member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.).

Cruz, however, intends to proceed with Wednesday's markup agenda. "We look forward to reporting her out tomorrow and suggest Senate Democrats weigh in with the White House on nominating Democrats to the unfilled spot," said Senate Commerce Committee spokesperson Blair Taylor.

A White House spokesperson didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

President Donald Trump nominated Severs, an aide to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, to an open GOP seat on the five-member agency this summer. Her confirmation would give Carr a 3-1 majority, and critics fear Trump could use that opportunity to oust Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat.

Democrats’ letter said Severs’ nomination should not be considered until the next Congress, when Democrats control the chamber, and paired with Gomez’s renomination. Their letter noted that the president has recently nominated Democrats to other boards and argued a bipartisan approach to nominations has “served both parties.” Gomez’s holdover time in her seat expires at the end of next year.

Carr has drawn pushback from Democrats and some Republicans like Cruz for his threats to media companies and fights over broadcast licensing — concerns Democrats alluded to in their letter.

“At last week’s Committee hearing, Senate Democrats voiced concerns about Ms. Thumann Severs’s close relationship with FCC Chairman Carr and how that would impact her support for Chairman Carr’s controversial policies, some of which you have opposed as well,” the letter said.

item.title: Capitol agenda: No quick exit from Dem leader brawl
item.description: Interviews with about a dozen Democratic senators and senior aides revealed Monday there is little appetite for their majority leader election — now on tap for Dec. 1 — to be moved up to this week.

media:content.media:title: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer looks on during a press conference on AI at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 23, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Senate Democrats may be settling in for a long and messy majority leader fight after Tuesday’s caucus lunch.

Interviews with about a dozen Democratic senators and senior aides revealed Monday there is little appetite for their majority leader election — now on tap for Dec. 1 — to be moved up to this week.

Expediting the closed-door vote had been floated by members eager to resolve the fight between Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Chris Van Hollen. Some privately express a desire to avoid being constantly pressed for public commitments in the race, and more wish to refocus on their governing agenda.

But members Monday appeared willing to tough it out for two more weeks.

“I would oppose expediting before we’ve had a full process,” said Sen. Jon Ossoff, who hasn’t backed a candidate.

The discussion will come to a head in the Senate Democratic lunch Tuesday — their first since Van Hollen threw his hat in the ring. A senator could call for a vote to waive caucus rules and hold the election sooner — though no one has publicly said they’ll do so. Schumer also has not called for the change, and Van Hollen has publicly opposed the move.

“It’s a family conversation that we’re going to have amongst ourselves,” Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester told reporters.

Moving up the vote would’ve been viewed as benefiting Schumer. While Schumer says he’s gathered the minimum 28 or 29 votes to win, only about 15 Democratic senators have publicly backed that support. Several others, granted anonymity to describe their intentions without courting public backlash, privately say they will support him.

Van Hollen has put his supporter count around 15, though his public endorsements so far remain in the single digits.

Otherwise, the public whip count has largely stagnated since last week — even as some senators praise the incumbent leader.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, for instance, made a coin-toss motion when asked who he’d support.

“Leave it to the Democrats that we flip nine seats, and the person who actually helps put it all together and do all that and all of a sudden, there’s a revolt,” he said, referring to Schumer.


What else we’re watching: 

— DUFFY’S $50B ASK GETS HILL REALITY CHECK — Senators are all but ruling out immediate approval of the Trump administration’s $50 billion request to overhaul the nation’s air traffic control system. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will be on Capitol Hill Tuesday to make his case to Republicans at their regular GOP weekly lunch following last week’s hourslong ground stop due to a malfunction of aviation communication infrastructure. Senate Majority Leader John Thune on Monday shot down the idea of muscling the money through Congress using a GOP-only reconciliation bill — instead raising the prospect of negotiating the funding with Democrats.
 
— GOP BALKS AT TALK OF HUANG RETURN — GOP lawmakers were wary of the suggestion that Jensen Huang should return to chipmaker Nvidia, despite Trump’s defense of the company’s former CEO. Nine GOP lawmakers, including members of Senate Banking and Foreign Affairs, rebuffed the suggestion that Huang should return following his ouster last week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Lawmakers also rejected pressure from powerful tech leaders who pushed for his reinstatement and a suggestion from the president that he’s learned his lesson. The comments from senior Republicans mark an emphatic break with Trump, who has maintained a close relationship with Huang.

Jordain Carney, Sam Ogozalek, Samuel Larreal, Katherine Long and Ari Hawkins contributed to this report.

item.title: Senate Democrats reject quick exit from Schumer vs. Van Hollen fight
item.description: A Tuesday caucus lunch will be just the beginning of a “family conversation” about the contentious race, senators say.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) speaks with reporters as he arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 16, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Senate Democrats are preparing for their all-consuming fight over who will lead them next year to drag on for weeks.

The contentious battle between Sens. Chuck Schumer of New York and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has already become, in the minds of some Democrats, a massive distraction from the work of preparing for a new majority and looming battles with President Donald Trump.

But interviews with about a dozen Democratic senators and senior aides Monday revealed little appetite to end the drama this week by moving up the closed-door election currently scheduled for Dec. 1.

“I would oppose expediting before we’ve had a full process,” said Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), who hasn’t backed a candidate.

Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), who is also publicly uncommitted, said, “I don’t think that’s going to happen.”

Moving up the vote would have been viewed as benefiting Schumer, the longtime top Democrat who said last week he had secured the votes for a second stint as majority leader. But Schumer has not called for changing the schedule, and Van Hollen is publicly opposed to any such move.

Given that, and the uproar among many Democratic voters unhappy with Schumer’s recent leadership, senators appear willing to tough it out for two more weeks. They include Schumer allies, Van Hollen diehards and the dozens of publicly undecided Senate Democrats — even as some privately express a desire to avoid being constantly pressed for public commitments in the race, and many more wish to refocus on their governing agenda.

Tuesday’s caucus lunch is the first time Senate Democrats will gather in person since Van Hollen announced his leadership bid Thursday night. A senator could use the opportunity to call for a vote to waive caucus rules and hold the election later this week. Instead, some Democrats said Tuesday they were simply hoping for a robust discussion.

“It’s a family conversation that we’re going to have amongst ourselves,” said Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.).

Van Hollen has been waging an unusually public campaign for leader that began with a cable-TV interview Thursday and has since expanded to include a “Chris for Leader” website and multiple Sunday talk show interviews. In an interview with POLITICO Sunday, he not only called for new leadership but also openly criticized Schumer’s record — pointing out, for instance, his opposition to the 2015 Iran nuclear deal that Trump later tore up.

“I’m really worried that we might blow what could be a huge opportunity to deliver,” Van Hollen said Monday, adding that he believes he has “momentum” in his supporter count.

Schumer, meanwhile, has focused almost solely on talking privately with colleagues since late last week — sticking to the traditional approach to a race that will be decided on a secret ballot of the 55 or 56 Democratic senators set to be sworn in early next year. He’s still viewed as the favorite due to the relationships he has built, funds he has raised and victories the party notched in this month’s midterms.

“I have a long history with Chuck,” said Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), who became the latest senator to publicly back Schumer Monday.

But scores of Senate Democrats are staying quiet. Coming out in support of Schumer would only put a target on their backs with some Democratic activists, who are ramping up an external pressure campaign on behalf of Van Hollen and remain furious over Schumer’s decision early in Trump’s second term to advance a GOP funding bill as well as his reluctance to cut off U.S. aid to Israel, among other issues.

While Schumer says he’s gathered the minimum 28 or 29 votes to win, only about 15 have publicly backed that support. Several others, granted anonymity to describe their intentions without courting public backlash, privately say they will support him. Van Hollen, meanwhile, has put his supporter count around 15, though his public endorsements so far remain in the single digits.

Otherwise, the public whip count has largely stagnated after an initial round of endorsements after Van Hollen jumped in last week — even as some senators conspicuously praise the incumbent leader.

Hickenlooper, for instance, made a coin-toss motion when asked who he was supporting. But he appeared to question why some Democrats were trying to ditch Schumer after they just outperformed even the rosiest election projections.

“Leave it to the Democrats that we flip nine seats, and the person who actually helps put it all together and do all that and all of a sudden, there's a revolt,” he said.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) also said he was undecided before listing Schumer’s assets: “Chuck delivered an amazing win. Chuck knows Trump, and that'll be really really important going forward.”

“No one, who is not on the ballot, worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” Kaine said before adding a third consideration: “Voters are demanding change.”

Several other veteran senators declined to state their voting intentions Monday. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who is expected to become Banking chair and is looking to move up the leadership ladder, did not respond to questions from reporters in the halls. Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), another member of leadership and a potential 2028 contender, used the same terms as Blunt Rochester, calling the matter a “family conversation.”

Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), who stopped just short of calling on Schumer to resign last year, dodged questions from reporters, while Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), who has been critical of Schumer and the DSCC’s approach to primaries, also said Monday he is in listening mode.

“I’m going to hear them both out, and I want to hear from the freshman class as well,” he said.

Katherine Tully-McManus and Calen Razor contributed to this report.

item.title: Ron Johnson holds out hope for 'relatively simple' GOP spending bill
item.description: The Senate Budget chair said he believed a new reconciliation package could start moving this week.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) pushes a button for an elevator as he is pursued by reporters after a vote at the U.S. Capitol on July 13, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson said he believed Republicans could pave the way for a final party-line spending bill before Democrats take control on Capitol Hill by putting a fiscal blueprint up for a vote later this week.

“I think what we're probably looking at is a relatively simple package that makes it pretty easy,” the Wisconsin Republican said. “I would hope we could pass a resolution this week.”

Johnson was noncommittal on the details — including whether it would include the $350 billion in defense funding that President Donald Trump called for last week — and reiterated that the committee is working through the details.

Asked about the possibility of a budget vote this week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said, "We'll see."

House Republicans sent the Senate a budget resolution that would unlock the party-line reconciliation process in July. It included only $74 billion in military funding in addition to farm aid and election integrity spending and has not advanced in the Senate.

Trump’s defense ask, Johnson said, “simplified the process,” but he acknowledged ongoing talks about possibly adding a debt ceiling hike to the proposal. Thune said "it’s obviously whatever we can get 50" votes to pass.

Pressed on when he might release text of a budget resolution, Johnson said, “Text is easy.”

The hard part, he added, is “deciding what can pass."

Jordain Carney contributed to this report.

item.title: Trump nominates top White House aide to head watchdog agency — as Democrats feared
item.description: The president has nominated Eric Ueland to head the Government Accountability Office.

media:content.media:title: Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump's pick to be deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget, appearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday.

item.dc:creator: By Katherine Tully-McManus, Jennifer Scholtes and Calen Razor
item.dc:contributor: By Katherine Tully-McManus, Jennifer Scholtes and Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump has nominated Eric Ueland as comptroller general and head of the Government Accountability Office, a position empowered to sue the administration on Congress’ behalf.

It marks the president’s last-ditch effort to get one of his allies confirmed to the post before Democrats take control of Congress in January. It also comes as lawmakers in both parties are calling for the independent oversight agency to challenge the Trump administration before the Supreme Court for withholding federal cash Congress has approved.

Ueland is currently the deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget, which is at the forefront of efforts to withhold and cancel federal funding. That makes him a pariah among Democrats who have already criticized Republicans of facilitating a “sham” confirmation process that breaks precedent for how the comptroller general is typically nominated.

And even though Ueland is generally popular among Republicans, his confirmation is not guaranteed. Some Senate Republicans are questioning whether it’s appropriate to confirm a sitting executive branch official to a position responsible for investigating and challenging the moves of that same administration.

“I think Eric's a really qualified individual, but I have concerns that this is the partisan pick for a very bipartisan office,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said in an interview Monday. “He's very qualified, but I think there's some strong partisan leanings on his part.”

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee will hold a hearing on his nomination Thursday — and the panel’s chair, Sen. Rand Paul, held off on a public endorsement Monday night.

“I stick with what I said last year about it. I think it's important to find someone who's honest and objective,” the Kentucky Republican said in a brief interview.

Paul then told reporters that the White House asked him to put Ueland’s name forward for the role. And asked if he pushed back on the administration, he said: “That's all I've got for you.”

Ueland is a known entity on Capitol Hill: He was a longtime Senate aide who spent time as staff director for Senate Budget Committee Republicans under then-Chair Michael Enzi of Wyoming, and was chief of staff to former Republican Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist.

He was also the White House director of legislative affairs during the first Trump administration, when he brokered talks on Capitol Hill between then-Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and senators to build an economic relief package that could clear the Senate as the Covid-19 pandemic bore down on U.S. markets.

Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) said Ueland is “seen as a straightforward, fair person that understands the operation of government and of agencies.”

“He's done so many different roles in so many different places,” Lankford said in an interview Monday, adding that he met with Ueland in his office a few months ago. “He has a good perspective of multiple agencies, and so I know where he's coming from.”

Still, Democrats and some Republicans have been eager for the agency to take the administration to court — something that could be politically difficult for someone in Ueland’s position to execute, given his relationships with top White House officials.

The agency, which has been operating under an acting comptroller general since last December, has issued more than a half-dozen findings of illegal impoundment of federal dollars since the start of Trump’s second term.

But so far, it has not taken legal action — even though the Supreme Court suggested last fall that GAO is the only entity with standing to sue the Trump administration for violating the decades-old Impoundment Control Act, which was designed to ensure presidents spend money Congress approves and exactly as lawmakers intended.

item.title: Phillip Swagel, longtime CBO director, will retire in January
item.description: Incoming Democratic leaders will get to select a replacement for nonpartisan fiscal scorekeeper.

media:content.media:title: Phillip Swagel, director of the Congressional Budget Office, testifies during a House committee hearing on the CBO's budget and economic outlook Feb. 14, 2024, on Capitol Hill in Washington.

item.dc:creator: By Katherine Tully-McManus
item.content:encoded:
Phillip Swagel, the longtime head of Congress’ nonpartisan scorekeeping agency, will leave Capitol Hill when his term is up in January, he said Monday.

His exit sets up a big decision for the Democratic leaders of the incoming Congress. Chairs of the House and Senate Budget committees are responsible for recommending a candidate for leading the agency, whom congressional leaders then appoint. That is expected to put Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) and Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) in charge of considering potential candidates.

Swagel, who has led the Congressional Budget Office since 2019, plans to return to academia and resume teaching economics at the University of Maryland. Swagel previously served as an assistant Treasury secretary under former President George W. Bush.

Swagel thanked past and present chairs and ranking members of the House and Senate Budget committees “for their support and guidance” during his term in his farewell message.

“I appreciate the many Members of Congress and staff who have relied on CBO to help inform their efforts on behalf of the nation,” Swagel said. “The time I have spent with Members has deepened my respect for their knowledge, thoughtfulness, and commitment to the people they represent.”

Swagel has maintained a productive relationship with GOP lawmakers in recent years despite their balking over the more than $4 trillion price tag he projected for the domestic policy megabill Republicans enacted last year.

The budget director accommodated the GOP’s decision to employ a controversial accounting tactic to estimate the cost of that bill, providing lawmakers with alternate projections that allowed them to claim the legislation would cost far less than under the traditional method — and sidestepped procedural headaches in the Senate.

Swagel this year also helped Republican lawmakers in their search for ways to root out “waste, fraud and abuse” in federal programs. The nonpartisan budget office worked with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to pinpoint cost-cutting policy changes, including spending money to crack down on fraud in payments to providers of skin substitutes.

Swagel’s office at CBO features a stuffed skunk, a gift from staff nodding to a long-running joke about CBO’s role as a voice of fiscal reality — the skunk at the legislative garden party.

Jennifer Scholtes contributed to this report.

item.title: Duffy, Bedford huddle with Congress following air system meltdown
item.description: The FAA chief briefed lawmakers Sunday; the Transportation secretary will be on the Hill Tuesday. "Key" members of government will meet at the White House today.

media:content.media:title: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy (right), with Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford at a news conference Saturday following a nationwide ground stop.

item.dc:creator: By Oriana Pawlyk
item.content:encoded:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford and other government officials are fanning out to brief Congress and the White House on Friday’s nationwide air system meltdown that led to a multihour ground stop.

Bedford held a virtual meeting with House and Senate members Sunday, while Duffy intends to speak to lawmakers at the Republican lunch Tuesday, according to a person familiar with the leaders’ fluid schedules, granted anonymity to speak candidly.

On Monday, Democrats on the House Transportation Committee, led by ranking member Rick Larsen (D-Wash.) said that committee staff will meet virtually on Tuesday with FAA and DOT officials for a briefing.

Separately, “key members of government” will be at the White House on Monday to discuss the ground stop and “how to prevent this situation from ever happening again,” a White House official said Monday and granted anonymity to discuss the planning.

Duffy is not expected to attend, the person said.

Duffy has spent months pitching the need for a new air traffic control system and previously told POLITICO he planned to head to Capitol Hill this week to lobby Congress for more funding for the “Brand New Air Traffic Control System,” the FAA’s long-sought modernization effort.

However, since the meltdown, Duffy has upped his ask from $30 billion to $50 billion. Duffy, who made the rounds on several Sunday talk shows, said it was still unclear whether Friday’s error happened due to incompetence or faulty equipment. The monthslong work is being done by L3Harris, a longtime contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration. The contractor is working to switch communications systems to fiber from the aging copper wire that serves dozens of facilities.

“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” L3Harris said in a statement Saturday, adding it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

Alex Gangitano contributed to this report.

item.title: Capitol agenda: Van Hollen takes the inside game outside
item.description: The Maryland senator’s outside pressure playbook could rally many in the party’s base and provide a template for what leadership bids become in the future.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen speaks during the Senate Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, Science and Related Agencies hearing on Capitol Hill, May 12, 2026, in Washington.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Chris Van Hollen may not ultimately win Senate majority leader, but he’s running a leadership race unlike any seen before.

Rather than focusing solely on the inside game of winning over his colleagues, the Maryland senator is mounting a very public bid against Minority Leader Chuck Schumer — forcing the Democratic caucus beyond private deliberations into a messy debate about their future.

The Maryland senator’s outside pressure playbook could rally many in the party’s base and transform the way these races are fought — and provide a template for what leadership bids become in the future.

His first test of success could come as soon as the party lunch Tuesday afternoon, when the discussion on whether or not to waive caucus rules and move up the leadership election to this week from Dec. 1 could come to a head.

Van Hollen told POLITICO Playbook in an interview Sunday he believes there’s enough support within the caucus to prevent the secret ballot election from happening this week. Schumer hasn’t yet weighed in on the idea.

“I think that there’s an overwhelming sentiment that we should have a fair and open process,” Van Hollen said. “I guess I would just ask why it would be that folks want to cut debate short. Is it because the longer this discussion goes on, the more our momentum grows?”

Van Hollen has otherwise been on a media run since announcing his bid against Schumer, including defending his “underdog” challenge while delivering remarks at Democrats’ “What’s Next” conference in Denver, Colorado.

He also launched a website over the weekend where supporters of his leadership bid submit their names and emails — a move that privately made some senators question whether his leadership challenge is a backdoor way to build up a 2028 presidential bid.

The email list, Van Hollen told Playbook, “is a way to get an early start for our Senate candidates in 2028. … The website allows people to contribute to the candidates.”

Schumer, meanwhile, continues to play the inside game after insisting he has the votes to win leader — even as some Democratic aides privately say they wish he’d mount a firmer public defense of himself. He’s still viewed as the favorite.

Among his backers are some senators who don’t like Van Hollen’s penchant for criticizing the party, according to two people granted anonymity to disclose private thinking.

Van Hollen tried to counter the notion this is about his own ambitions rather than the party’s welfare, telling reporters Friday he is no longer pursuing a 2028 presidential run.

But one Schumer-neutral Democrat said Van Hollen’s credibility had already taken a hit: “The damage is done.”

Read much more from the interview with Van Hollen in Playbook later this morning, including his thoughts on who Democrats should pick to lead them in the House.

What else we’re watching: 

— FIRST IN IC: CANTWELL TARGETS LUTNICK ON CHIPS — Senate Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of failing to keep sensitive tech out of the hands of U.S. adversaries. Cantwell’s letter Sunday offers a glimpse into how the panel’s top Democrat will conduct committee business and oversight in the new Congress, when she returns as chair. It also spotlights the increasing bipartisan fury aimed at the ally of President Donald Trump after allegations his department failed to properly enforce export controls even after learning that top chipmaker Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang was in a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

— FIRST IN IC: PALLONE’S E&C PLANS — Incoming House Energy and Commerce Chair Frank Pallone’s legislative and oversight agenda could start with data centers. The New Jersey Democrat, in a phone interview Friday, outlined his plan of action after visiting frustrated residents in Memphis kept up late at night by the loud churn of new data centers being built by Elon Musk. Pallone wants to haul in tech CEOs and EPA officials to testify before his panel in the next Congress. He’s also crafting legislation that would impose “very strong federal guardrails” for data centers, including by requiring more local input before developers can start building them or ensuring the power generation is paid for by companies themselves.

Jordain Carney, Will Steakin and Kelsey Brugger contributed to this report.

item.title: The 2 Texans competing to be Trump’s top defender in the House
item.description: Whoever gets the job will be tasked with rebutting arguments and defending the administration from Democrats’ investigative onslaught.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Pat Fallon (R-Texas) speaks during a House Oversight and Government Reform Committee hearing on sanctuary cities on Capitol Hill March 5, 2025. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
As House Democrats pledge an all-out investigative blitz against President Donald Trump and his administration, two Texas Republicans are duking it out to be the president's chief defender on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee.

Rep. Pat Fallon, 58, a former Notre Dame football player and Air Force veteran who served in the Texas state Legislature before coming to Congress in 2021, is squaring up against Rep. Brandon Gill, 32, a Dartmouth College graduate who worked as an investment banker on Wall Street before his 2022 election.

While Democrats are planning to use their new subpoena power and agenda-setting authority to go after Trump across all committees and both chambers, the Oversight Committee is where some of the most aggressive investigations could take place. The panel’s incoming chair, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, put the executive branch on notice the night Democrats took control of Congress with two words: “Lawyer up.”

Whoever gets the job of top Oversight Republican will be at the front lines of rebutting Democratic attacks against the president and his allies. With these high stakes, Republicans will have to decide which of the two contenders they trust more to deploy the best messaging campaign and strategy for defending Trump.

In many ways, Gill and Fallon are similar. Both are staunch conservatives from the same congressional delegation as well as impressive fundraisers for the House GOP's campaign arm: Fallon brought in over $1.7 million for the House Republican campaign arm this year so far while Gill raked in more than $1.9 million.

They also have similar perspectives on what Democrats are threatening to accomplish in their majority and how that would inform their posture on the dais.

Fallon said in an interview he expects Democrats to seize on “a fabricated reason to impeach the president, and they will start with him and work toward Elon Musk, the administration, Cabinet secretaries, anybody who gave money to Trump and whom they don't agree with.”

Gill, in a separate interview, agreed Republicans must be prepared for Democrats to escalate what he says they’re already doing: “weaponizing the committee to go after conservatives, conservative donors — and we need to counter that.”

But the two have distinct styles and selling points. Fallon, the longer-serving member, touts himself as more battle-tested, plus he knows what it’s like to be a member of the minority. He also has policy expertise, having advanced major provisions of the national defense package as chair of the House Armed Services subcommittee on Military Personnel.

“I am a better member of Congress because of my experience and expertise from my time in the Texas House and Senate. That has made me a better member, and I have the experience to handle the committee,” Fallon said.

Those credentials are resonating with some of Fallon’s boosters.

“Freshmen don't have the background, relationships or the legislative experience needed,” said one senior House Republican who like others in this story was granted anonymity to speak candidly about their colleagues.

Another senior GOP member who supports Fallon noted, "There's a reason why lieutenants don't command. They don't have the breadth and depth of experience to do the job. Gill has some maturing to do to step into the role of the leader, but Fallon already has the experience.”

Gill rejects that premise. He highlights his ability to message to the base and reach the masses through viral moments shared with his over 300,000 X followers.

He said his current role as chair of an Oversight GOP task force on “Defending Constitutional Rights and Exposing Institutional Abuses” gives him “leadership experience right now,” adding that “one of the things that separate Democrats from Republicans is Democrats are far more willing to elevate people based on seniority and Republicans operate on a meritocracy.”

For whoever gets the job, it will come down to who can win a closed-door vote in the coming weeks inside the House GOP Steering Committee, which is made up of party leaders and members representing the interests of different regions. Fallon is a current member of the Steering Committee, which could help his standing in the room — though its composition could be drastically different due to midterm losses.

One former House GOP aide who remains familiar with Republican Conference dynamics predicted Gill would have the edge.

“Fallon has more experience in Congress,” that person said, “but Gill benefits in that he has a national profile and is a proven communicator for a committee that will be the center of attention next Congress. He can also energize the base that Republicans will need to turn out in future elections.”

Gill also has a strong connection to Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), his role model in Congress who had a stint as Oversight chair before winning the Judiciary gavel. He is now preparing to be House minority leader in the next Congress.

“We need the committee to be filled with the best communicators we have in a way that resonantes with the American people and who can go toe-to-toe with Garcia,” said Gill. “And frankly, that’s what I’m looking to do.”

A senior House Republican and Gill supporter said the party needs “a great communicator” who can “fight back, and that’s an easy pick: It’s not who’s next in the line, it’s who is the best in the line and it’s all about having the best players on the field.

“Brandon,” the member continued, “is the best communicator in the Republican Party. If you watch how he grills witnesses — in the minority we’re going to need that.”

item.title: House Democrats want Trump out of office. They don’t know if impeachment is the answer.
item.description: While some Democrats say the president has committed impeachable offenses, they’re worried a headlong rush would simply die in the Senate and derail their agenda.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) speaks alongside advocates during a press conference on a petition to impeach and remove President Donald Trump outside the U.S. Capitol July 23, 2025. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette, Kyle Cheney and Riley Rogerson
item.dc:contributor: By Chris Marquette, Kyle Cheney and Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
A growing number of House Democrats say they’re open to using their new majority to impeach President Donald Trump — but they’re concerned that a rush job could backfire.

After two attempts to remove the president during the first Trump administration, many members are heeding advice from colleagues who led those previous battles and say a third attempt must be methodical or risk playing into the weakened president’s hands.

“I think Donald Trump would love us to organize a campaign of impeachment against him right now because he thinks that's his last hope for rallying the dwindling MAGA base at this point,” said Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who is poised to lead the House Judiciary Committee next year and ran the impeachment trial against Trump over the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol.

Indeed, Trump has previously declared that his first two impeachments benefited him politically and said recently he would welcome the prospect of a third.

“I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that, because it would be impeachment for no reason,” he said to reporters a day after the GOP’s midterm drubbing. “For what? For having a successful country?”

Trump’s comment hits on another fundamental dilemma for Democrats: What, precisely, would a new round of impeachment articles against Trump say? While Democrats have accused him of wide-ranging corruption — self-enrichment, accepting foreign gifts, granting pay-for-play pardons, abusing power to target his enemies and launching an illegal war in Iran — there is no consensus about what charges a Democratic House would level, or what type of investigation would precede formal action.

Interviews with 14 House Democrats from across the ideological spectrum reveal a desire to proceed with varying degrees of caution as party leaders plot the next two years in power ahead of the next presidential election, when Trump will be term-limited out of office anyway.

Some Democrats say the chamber should prioritize policy fights rather than impeachment — including Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.) who led the now-defunct Jan. 6 committee that concluded Trump presented a unique danger to the republic.

“Impeachment is not a priority for me,” said Thompson, the likely next chair of the Homeland Security committee. “If other members file a resolution and it gets to the floor, I'll vote for it.”

Many Democrats worry that dragging the country through divisive and time-consuming impeachment proceedings could prove futile if they don’t first lay the groundwork to persuade the public that such an exercise is necessary.

And even a perfectly executed process would run into a math problem: It takes two-thirds of the Senate to convict a president in an impeachment trial, meaning Democrats would need at least 11 Republicans to join them for a conviction — a threshold they failed to clear even in the days after the Jan. 6 riot.

Raskin noted the tricky “constitutional arithmetic,” and he’s not alone.

“Is the Senate going to convict? You need to weigh that in and whether to proceed,” said Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.), who served with Thompson and Raskin on the Jan. 6 committee. She was also an impeachment manager in 2020, when Democrats sought to remove Trump on grounds he threatened to withhold foreign aid to Ukraine unless president Volodymyr Zelenskyy agreed to investigate his political enemies.

“I think we need a national conversation,” Lofgren added.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) was even more blunt: “No,” he said when asked whether the House should impeach Trump. “I'm a former prosecutor. You don't indict somebody if you don't think you can convict.”

Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be speaker in January and was himself a manager in the Ukraine-related impeachment trial, has so far taken a cautious approach to the issue.

“I haven't had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment,” Jeffries said a day after the midterms. “We've been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability.”

When asked Thursday if Trump has committed impeachable offenses, Jeffries dodged: “As I've repeatedly indicated, we haven't ruled anything in. We haven't ruled anything out. We're going to follow the facts. We're going to apply the law. We're going to be guided by the Constitution, and we're going to let the chips fall where they may.”

Jeffries’ approach tracks closely with that of his predecessor Nancy Pelosi, who as speaker resisted early pressure from Democrats to rush toward impeachment after they took the majority in 2019. Though some members were then eager to impeach Trump over allegations stemming from the investigation of his contacts with Russia, Pelosi insisted that the chamber wait to build a clear case to the public that impeachment was warranted.

Her calculus changed when a whistleblower informed Congress about Trump’s dealings with Zelenskyy. Some Democratic lawmakers are convinced that Trump’s penchant for escalation against his adversaries could give them fresh fodder for impeachment in the next Congress.

“We'll see what the next two years bring in terms of what Trump does,” said Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) in an interview. “Because I also do worry that he's going to get more and more desperate and more and more volatile, and who knows what actions he may take that just become impossible to ignore when it comes to impeachment.”

But Ansari also acknowledged the potential for a strategic blunder in rushing headlong into the process: “I am torn on it. I believe that he should be impeached, but I also hear the concerns of colleagues, especially ones who were here and have been through that. That perhaps that would suck the oxygen in a way that is not the most effective.”

Another deterrent for Democrats: A quick impeachment in the House would trigger a Senate trial that would grind Washington to a halt, just as Democrats are attempting to make good on their promises to prioritize affordability for Americans. Presidential impeachments instantly displace other Senate business and even typically requires the chief justice of the Supreme Court to preside.

At the same time, Democratic leaders will also have to deal with a faction that remains driven to impeach Trump quickly, who argue that slow-walking proceedings in the face of impeachable offenses would be risky in a different way.

“It's setting a dangerous precedent when people [are] like, ‘no, it's a distraction.’ What are you talking about?” said Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.), who famously rankled party leaders by declaring her intent to “impeach the motherfucker” just days after taking office in 2019. “This won't be the last president that runs businesses out of the Oval Office.”

Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) also said Democrats shouldn’t be afraid to stand their ground: “If there is something that is worthy of impeachment, we should have impeachment, even if it's bad politics.”

Democrats also need to be attuned to voters who may want to see the party hold Trump accountable, said Rep. Becca Balint (D-Vt.), while noting she would vote for an impeachment resolution on the floor.

“There's definitely a core of our base that wants revenge and vengeance, right? And there's another group, actually, that just wants to make sure that the Constitution will hold, and that they feel like if [Trump] is allowed to get away with this without a third impeachment, then what does that say about the system?” she said in an interview.

Ultimately, Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), who served as a manager in Trump’s first trial, said it was important to remember that impeachment is just one option for holding the president accountable.

“Impeachment has taken on this almost mythical place in American culture because people know about it. But it's a tool. It's not an end in and of itself,” he said. “I've done it before … and if I thought that was appropriate, I would do it again. But right now, we have to see what type of coalition we can put together.”

item.title: Van Hollen disputes Schumer’s claim that he has the votes to stay leader
item.description: The Maryland Democrat says his support is growing as senators privately discuss moving up the Dec. 1 leadership vote.

media:content.media:title: “I think there's a very open lane here. The Schumer team's put out a lot of misinformation,” Chris Van Hollen said.

item.dc:creator: By Jalen Beckford
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen on Sunday accused Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer’s team of trying to scare Senate Democrats away from backing his bid for majority leader, pushing back on Schumer’s claim that he already has the votes to stay in charge.

“I think there's a very open lane here. The Schumer team's put out a lot of misinformation,” Van Hollen said on ABC's “This Week.” “They're essentially trying to instill fear in people who may say that they're going to support me as a new leader. But that's part of the problem. That's part of the old system.”

Van Hollen didn’t specify on ABC what misinformation he was referring to. In a separate interview on “Fox News Sunday,” he claimed Schumer’s team had circulated a list that counted some of his own supporters as votes for Schumer.

Schumer’s team hasn’t released a whip list, and Schumer said in a statement Thursday that he had the votes to remain leader. Van Hollen told Fox he has the support of “about 15 and growing,” up from the more than 10 he cited Thursday.

Van Hollen also told CNN that he saw talk of moving up the Dec. 1 leadership election as a “sign of weakness” and accused Schumer’s team of seeking an earlier vote. Schumer hasn’t publicly weighed in on the timing.

Senate Democrats have privately discussed holding the vote before Thanksgiving recess, as POLITICO reported Friday. One option would be for a senator to raise the issue at Tuesday’s caucus lunch. An earlier vote would require Democrats to waive caucus rules, and even some Schumer allies are skeptical it will happen.

Asked on ABC why Democrats should replace Schumer after taking back the Senate, Van Hollen pointed to Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s recent win as an example, noting that Washington Democrats were late to get behind Colom’s campaign.

“Look, I respect the work of the DSCC. And I used to chair the DSCC and the DCCC in the House,” Van Hollen said. “But let's be real. This was not a Washington-orchestrated election around the country. This was the American people rising up against a lawless president and demanding change.” Colom on NBC's "Meet the Press" said he didn't know which Democrat he would support.

Van Hollen launched his challenge Thursday. Schumer remains favored, with public backing from Democratic Sens. Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Angela Alsobrooks (Md.) and Kirsten Gillibrand (N.Y.). Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed are backing Van Hollen, and Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan joined them Friday.

CORRECTION: An earlier version of this story misstated that POLITICO had reached out to Sen. Schumer’s office for comment.

item.title: Dems can win more in Mississippi if they spend money, Scott Colom says
item.description: "There wasn't a bunch of campaign money spent to win Mississippi, compared to other states," the senator-elect said.

media:content.media:title: Scott Colom talks on the phone at his campaign office in Jackson, Mississippi, on Nov. 11, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By David Cohen
item.content:encoded:
Sen.-elect Scott Colom said Sunday that Democrats need to invest more resources in Mississippi so that his surprise election to the Senate doesn't prove to be a one-time event.

Speaking on NBC's "Meet the Press," Colom said, "We didn't have a bunch of resources. There wasn't a bunch of campaign money spent to win Mississippi, compared to other states. But that meant we did it the Mississippi way, and I'm proud of that. What we need to do now, as a Democratic Party, is understand we can't continue to allow that lack of investment to occur."

Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in one of 2026's most surprising elections. Democrats, at this point, have also picked up Senate seats in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, and may still win the seat in Alaska.

He added: "We need to put senators like myself in position where we can deliver for the rural South, where we can be leaders in ways that show the voters in rural America that we care about them, the voters in the Deep South that we want them to be successful."

Colom will be the first Black senator to serve from Mississippi since Hiram Revels (1870-71) and Blanche Kelso Bruce (1875-81) in the Reconstruction era. During the 20th century, Mississippi elected a number of the most avowedly segregationist lawmakers in Washington, including Sens. James Vardaman, Theodore G. Bilbo and James Eastland.

In an interview with host Kristen Welker, Colom spoke of the things he hoped to accomplish in the Senate, including raising the minimum wage, pushing for affordable health care, and putting Congress back in charge of tariff policy instead of the president.

"What we have to understand is the Constitution's clear. Tariffs are supposed to be determined in Congress. And I'll tell you, as I, you know, talk to more and more of the new Democratic senators and the ones that are currently in the Senate, everybody's in agreement that we've got to get the tariff policy back," Colom said.

He declined to say whether he would support New York's Chuck Schumer, the current minority leader, or Maryland's Chris Van Hollen for Senate majority leader.

"I've got to be honest with you," Colom told Welker, "I don't know either one of them that well. So, I'm going to listen to what other people tell me about them and I'm going to figure out what are the things that people are doing well in leadership, what are the things they're not doing well, and find out how we can work together to achieve results."

item.title: Kirsten Gillibrand is dreaming of a Democratic supermajority
item.description: They could be as little as four seats away from a filibuster-proof Senate margin, and the DSCC chair sees paths to getting there in 2028.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) departs a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 12, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Democrats have improbably won at least 55 Senate seats in the upcoming Congress. Kirsten Gillibrand is already looking for a path to a filibuster-proof 60.

The Senate Democratic campaign chair, in an interview with POLITICO after last week’s sweeping wins, laid out the possibility of flipping seven more seats in 2028, when the party faces a more favorable map but could also face a referendum on their own leadership in Congress after two years in power.

Such a feat would give Democrats a Senate supermajority capable of defeating GOP attempts to block major bills. Coupled with a presidential win and a House majority, it would give them a level of unilateral power in Washington unseen since 2010, when President Barack Obama signed major health care and financial regulation overhauls.

Gillibrand pointed to several states President Donald Trump won three times that Democrats plan to heavily target, including Iowa, South Carolina and Kansas. Democrats flipped seats in those three states last week, and she also named Alaska — where they are optimistic they will unseat GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan once all the votes are counted.

Gillibrand also pointed to more traditional swing states including Wisconsin, where Democrats just swept state government, and North Carolina, where they took back retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis’ seat, as “the two bluest states that are in play” that Democrats would “absolutely” target.

“All of those states will now be states that we're going to be hoping to find the best candidates, getting them early, organizing the grassroots early, trying to help state parties raise money so that they can actually organize,” Gillibrand said.

Democrats could also try to go back after some of the near-misses. Gillibrand mentioned Florida, where some in the party have publicly criticized leaders for not devoting considerable resources to what ended up being a closer-than-expected race.

Both Gillibrand and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer brushed off any second-guessing in the days after the election about Florida, an expensive state that would have required Democrats to pour in potentially hundreds of millions of dollars across several media markets.

“We had a big map, and we tried to maximize the number of states we could win,” Schumer said in an interview last week in his Capitol Hill office, while Gillibrand said in a separate interviewthat “you would have needed Texas-sized money to win in Florida.”

Democrats will also have to play defense in a number of states. Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown, who won his comeback special-election bid last week, must run again in 2028, and fellow Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, the incoming Senate GOP campaign chair, warned Brown about his Washington home search this week: “Make sure you rent, do not buy."

Moreno and Senate Republican Leader John Thune met this week to start plotting out their own 2028 strategy. Though the map is viewed as more favorable to Democrats, Republicans are hoping the party overreaches with voters or gets mired in infighting, creating opportunities for GOP pickups.

In addition to Ohio, Democrats will need to defend seats in Georgia, Nevada, Colorado and Arizona — states that Republicans are all but guaranteed to make major investments. Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman is also up for reelection. He hasn’t said yet if he’s running, but he is likely to face a challenge if he enters the Democratic primary.

Gillibrand is preparing to volunteer for a second term as chair of the Senate Democratic campaign arm. So far, she faces no competition for the job but is making an emphatic case for another tour of duty.

She pointed to early recruitments of top-tier candidates such as former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Brown in Ohio, investing early in key states and a partywide focus on rising costs as lessons from 2026 that she believes Democrats should carry over into 2028.

Many progressives have criticized the DSCC and Schumer’s primary strategy, accusing them of tilting the playing field against more left-leaning candidates. Most notably, Schumer backed Rep. Haley Stevens in a fierce Michigan primary, only for her to lose and then turn on the party’s hard-left nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, in the final days of the election.

Asked about changes to the DSCC’s primary strategy, Gillibrand did not answer directly but said that in states like Maine and Michigan, it largely focused early on attacking Republicans, not boosting particular Democrats.

“The DSCC doesn't really have a primary strategy. If it's a blue state, we really let all flowers bloom,” she said. “If the state's going to be a winning state for Democrats, we don't worry at all.”

item.title: ‘A long conversation’: Senate Democrats gird for protracted Schumer-Van Hollen fight
item.description: The leadership battle has sparked frustration within the caucus, and there’s talk about trying to bring it to a close next week.

media:content.media:title: Senate Democrats' post-election glow has been dulled by the challenge to Sen. Chuck Schumer (center).

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney, Irie Sentner and Adam Wren
item.dc:contributor: By Jordain Carney, Irie Sentner and Adam Wren
item.content:encoded:
DENVER — Senate Democrats are bracing for an intense, messy, distracting fight over whether Chuck Schumer or Chris Van Hollen should lead them come January.

Less than 24 hours into the battle Friday, it was already sucking up attention in Washington and in Denver, where many prominent Democrats — including Van Hollen — have gathered to discuss how to wield their new power come January.

“We’re going to have a long conversation about what the caucus should look like,” Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), who is backing Schumer, told reporters in Colorado when asked about the leadership election.

Sen. Cory Booker, a member of Senate Democratic leadership, said in an interview Friday that “my phone has been blowing up.” And his fellow New Jersey Democrat, Sen. Andy Kim, who like Booker isn’t publicly backing the longtime New York leader or the Maryland upstart, is offering some advice on the leadership fight: Keep it clean.

“Regardless of how this unfolds, I hope we can do it in a way that tries our best to preserve our unity,” Kim said in an interview. “As we move forward, I just urge that we do our best to make sure that we’re respectful of each other.”

That plea comes as senators prepare to face a mountain of outside pressure ahead of the Dec. 1 contest. High-profile House Democrats, who have no role in determining who leads the Senate but influence massive online followings, are weighing in. And progressive outside groups are ramping up their existing pressure campaign on senators to either oppose Schumer, who is the favorite in the race, or push them to openly support Van Hollen.

Inside the Capitol, some Senate Democrats privately worry it’s exactly the wrong time to have a messy leadership fight, according to several people granted anonymity to describe private conversations.

Emboldened by their election wins, the party is trying to iron out its agenda and have bills ready to go on the floor once members are sworn in early next year. Democrats also need to figure out their strategy for a looming Dec. 11 funding deadline as they face pressure to either cut off funding for the Iran war or shut down the government.

“We are having a vigorous debate about the right mix of experience, capabilities, and vision, but this should not distract us from delivering on the urgent needs of our constituents,” Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) wrote in a social media post Friday, publicly echoing a sentiment that is bouncing around the caucus.

Kim added, “I’ll be honest — if we don’t have the right agenda, no matter who’s leader, it’s not going to get done.”

There’s frustration in corners of the caucus toward Van Hollen, according to three Democratic aides, that he has injected division into what should have been a unifying moment. Van Hollen, and his supporters, in turn, argue his leadership bid is aimed at delivering exactly what voters want: a change.

Booker said that Van Hollen has “absolutely earned the right to run,” but also credited Schumer as the quarterback of the Democrats’ Senate campaign push: “We just won a very big game, and you’ve got to give a lot of credit to his leadership.”

Democrats are privately discussing moving up the leadership election to next week, four of the people granted anonymity said. It’s not yet decided if that will happen, but one potential scenario would be for a senator to call for a vote on rescheduling it when Democrats meet for their caucus lunch Tuesday. Senators could hold the leadership vote later in the week before leaving for a weeklong Thanksgiving recess.

Even some Schumer allies are skeptical it will be moved up, though, and there’s confusion in other corners about whether Senate Democratic rules dictating the timing of the leadership election can be overruled.

Those rules say the election cannot be held before December but they can be waived. A waiver vote would be conducted by secret ballot, according to a person with knowledge of the matter, which could help take pressure off Democratic senators wary of public backlash.

Senate Democrats are already beginning to meet privately to start debating their agenda for the new Congress. Senators are set to hold a teleconference Saturday to hear from incoming freshmen and the soon-to-be chairs of the several key committees to hear about their priorities, according to a copy of the invite obtained by POLITICO. The meeting was scheduled before Van Hollen jumped into the race.

But it’s the leadership race that is now front and center. Schumer and Van Hollen are both talking privately to colleagues, and, according to Van Hollen, they’ve also spoken to each other.

Schumer claimed in a statement Thursday that he has the votes to win the election, and Democratic senators and aides broadly agree. Several Democratic senators have publicly backed Schumer in the past day, including Sens. Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin, Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada. Several other senators, granted anonymity given the sensitivity of the race, have told POLITICO in recent weeks that they intend to back Schumer.

Van Hollen has acknowledged repeatedly that he is the “underdog” in the election. He said Thursday night that he had the support of more than 10 senators; Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon both threw their support behind him Friday.

But Senate Democratic insiders believe he will struggle to approach the 28 or 29 votes he will need to win — and some question if he can hit 20. Most Democrats, they say, are OK with two more years of Schumer’s leadership and, like Booker, believe he deserves some credit for the sweeping election win.

Van Hollen has faced internal doubts that his leadership ambitions are anything more than a dalliance meant to draw attention for a future presidential bid. He said Friday he no longer plans to run for the White House in 2028 and was sincere about leading the Senate.

“We understand that this will be a competition,” Van Hollen told reporters Friday in Denver. “I think it's important to give Senate Democrats a choice.”

Sentner and Wren reported from Denver. Carney reported from Washington. Meredith Lee Hill in Washington contributed to this report.

item.title: MAGA firebrand Lauren Boebert falls to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in Colorado
item.description: Boebert was denied a fourth term in the House.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) looks on during a House Oversight and Government Reform Committee hearing in the U.S. Capitol on March 4, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Alec Hernandez
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) is the latest to fall in Democrats’ blue wave.

Boebert, the conservative firebrand who's drawn national attention, fell to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in Colorado's 4th District and was denied a fourth term in the House.
