item.title: Brian Poindexter, incoming House Democrat, is under investigation for sexual harassment
item.description: The DCCC and Poindexter's campaign have opened separate probes into the Ohio ironworker.

media:content.media:title: Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter (D-Ohio) arrives at the AC Hotel during new member orientation in Washington on Nov. 8, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation over the alleged sexual harassment of a campaign worker, House Democrats and his own campaign said Friday — days after POLITICO reported two Democratic groups had taken his name off their websites.

The House Democratic campaign arm has hired an outside firm to investigate “allegations” against Poindexter, its top staffer said in a statement. And a spokesperson for the incoming Ohio freshman's campaign said it had initiated its own external review while characterizing Poindexter's actions as innocuous and misunderstood.

“Brian gave what he thought was an innocuous compliment to a volunteer. He heard later that it made her feel uncomfortable and he felt awful,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

“When Brian learned about this, we immediately began to work to get to the bottom of it with an outside HR firm,” the spokesperson added. “Neither Brian nor the campaign ever wants anyone to feel uncomfortable.”

DCCC Executive Director Julie Merz said her group "has been made aware of the allegations and takes them seriously."

"In the interest of fairness to all parties involved, we have hired an independent, third-party firm to investigate any instance of inappropriate behavior, conduct interviews and gather the facts,” she said in a Friday statement. “Upon completion of that investigation, which we have asked to be swift, thorough and transparent, the DCCC will have further comment.”

POLITICO has not confirmed details of the allegation against Poindexter. Punchbowl News previously reported the DCCC statement.

Poindexter defeated Republican Rep. Max Miller in a Cleveland-area district after a heated race that garnered national attention. Miller faced allegations of domestic abuse related to his divorce which he denies.

The news of the investigation into Poindexter comes after the political arms of the moderate Blue Dog Coalition and Congressional Progressive Caucus removed their endorsements of Poindexter around Election Day without prior explanation. They confirmed Friday that they "became aware of a report of alleged sexual harassment in the final days of the campaign."

“We informed the DCCC and connected the individual with legal advocacy and support services so she could determine how she wanted to proceed," the Blue Dog PAC and CPC PAC said in a joint statement, which further indicated that the woman who made the complaint "requested that we did not disclose any details about this publicly" to protect her identity and to give her time to determine her next steps.

"We respected her desires, and also felt we needed to immediately pull our endorsements pending the investigation being completed," the statement continued. "The investigation is ongoing and we await the results."

When asked about the endorsements Tuesday during a brief interview on Capitol Hill, Poindexter said, “My main focus right now is just setting up my office and stuff. There could be time to join ideological caucuses.”

He added, “Nothing to read into that. Just, I’m waiting to learn the political landscape.”

The campaign spokesperson said Friday, “As a lifelong ironworker, Brian always went out of his way to make everyone feel comfortable on any job site. He knows these are different worlds, but he will do the same in Congress.”

item.title: Pressley's plans
item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
As progressive groups search for an alternative to Hakeem Jeffries for speaker, Massachusetts Rep. Ayanna Pressley’s name is bouncing around online circles. Asked if she is considering a bid, her spokesperson Ricardo Sánchez pointed to ongoing discussions Pressley is having.

“Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment, and deliver for the people,” he said in a statement. “She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership.”

item.title: Virginia Democrats back Scott’s bid for House education gavel
item.description: The support comes as Rep. Bobby Scott faces two challengers for the top slot. He has led committee Democrats for more than a decade.

media:content.media:title: The Virginia House delegation said Rep. Bobby Scott is “well suited” to hold the Trump administration "accountable."

item.dc:creator: By Bianca Quilantan
item.content:encoded:
Seven Virginia Democrats on Friday said they are backing Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.) to lead the House Education and Labor committee next Congress.

Reps. Don Beyer, Jennifer McClellan, Suhas Subramanyam, Eugene Vindman and James Walkinshaw, along with Reps.-elect Elaine Luria and Shannon Taylor, in a statement, urged the Democratic caucus to reappoint Scott to the position as he faces two opponents.

Reps. Suzanne Bonamici (D-Ore.) and Jahana Hayes (D-Conn.) are challenging Scott for the top slot. He has led committee Democrats for more than a decade.

“Nobody else is better positioned to hold the Trump Administration accountable for dismantling the Department of Education and eroding the civil rights of students,” the Virginia lawmakers wrote. “His leadership during the past two years helped shine a light on what this administration has done ahead of our historic midterm victories.”

The Virginia House delegation also said Scott is “well suited” to hold the secretaries of Labor and Health and Human Services accountable.

Earlier this month, Scott sent a letter to agency heads, making his oversight stance known as he fights for the committee’s top job. He demanded that the agency heads, including Education Secretary Linda McMahon, guarantee they will preserve documents. He warned that officials and employees who violate the law “are subject to criminal penalties.”

The Virginia Democrats also lauded Scott’s understanding of the federal budget process and his knowledge of civil rights laws and the Constitution. And they touted his efforts to fund K-12 schools and bolster funding for historically Black colleges and universities when he previously held the gavel.

“We strongly encourage House Democrats to re-appoint Bobby Scott as Chair of the House Committee on Education & Labor because of his dedication, his ability and proven record to hit the ground running to rein in the Trump Administration,” they wrote. “As Chair, Bobby Scott will deliver for America’s students, workers, and families.”

item.title: Hakeem Jeffries eases into committee term-limit debate: ‘The right conversation to have’
item.description: Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.) is proposing a four-term cap for Democratic panel leaders.

media:content.media:title: Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries did not outright endorse term limits.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries stepped gingerly into the debate over placing term limits on Democratic committee chairs Friday, calling it “the right discussion” as a fierce generational-change fight roils his caucus.

“It's the right conversation to have, and we're going to have that discussion in December as a caucus, and I look forward to embracing it,” Jeffries said.

While Jeffries did not outright endorse term limits, his openness to discussing restrictions on committee leadership is noteworthy as House Democrats consider rules to govern themselves in the next Congress.

Several committee leaders are fighting the idea, with Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat and a key Jeffries ally, calling himself "diametrically opposed” this week.

Jeffries was asked about a proposal from Rep. Susie Lee of Nevada that would establish a four-term limit on the top Democrats on committees. Speaking at Majority Democrats’ “What’s Next” conference Friday, he said he plans to speak with Lee about her pitch tomorrow.

“We'll see where she goes with it,” he said. “But I think it's the right discussion, and it's a discussion that we're going to have.”

item.title: Jack Smith calls Senate Republican’s bar complaint against him a ‘political stunt’
item.description: Smith said a complaint by Tennessee Republican Sen. Bill Hagerty was meant to punish him a day after his September testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee.

media:content.media:title: Former Justice Department special counsel Jack Smith testifies before the Senate Judiciary Committee at the Capitol on Sept. 29, 2026, in Washington.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette and Kyle Cheney
item.dc:contributor: By Chris Marquette and Kyle Cheney
item.content:encoded:
Jack Smith, the former special counsel who prosecuted President Donald Trump, is calling a GOP senator’s bid to seek his disbarment a “retaliatory political stunt” that misstates the scope of Congress’ immunity from prosecutorial scrutiny and relies on selectively leaked documents.

In a Nov. 3 letter to Tennessee bar discipline officials, reviewed by POLITICO, Smith said a complaint by Tennessee Republican Sen. Bill Hagerty was meant to punish Smith a day after his September testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee.

That public hearing largely backfired for Republicans and gave Smith a forum to rebut their claims that he acted inappropriately in his investigation of Trump for seeking to subvert the 2020 election. The next day, Hagerty wrote to the Board of Professional Responsibility of the Supreme Court of Tennessee asking for the body to revoke Smith’s law license, citing Smith’s moves to access the phone records of Hagerty and other GOP lawmakers in the days surrounding Trump’s effort to prevent Congress from certifying his loss to Joe Biden on Jan. 6, 2021.

Republican senators have been particularly incensed that Smith obtained a court order that prohibited their phone service providers from informing them they had had their call logs subpoenaed; those logs did not include the content of the messages but did reveal who the lawmakers called or texted around the time of the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol.

They have argued that those "nondisclosure orders” violate the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause, which prohibits legal or criminal action against members of Congress for their official work. Senators have also complained that Smith never informed the judge who issued the orders that he was seeking the records of members.

In their letter, Smith’s lawyers called the bar complaint “meritless” and an effort that “retaliates against Mr. Smith’s exercise of his right to free speech.” They also contend that the Speech or Debate Clause only protects members from being compelled to testify or face criminal consequences for their legislative work. A secret subpoena for phone records does not trigger those limitations, they said.

In addition, Smith’s team emphasized that the secrecy order was intended to prevent Trump — who was criminally charged with obstruction and had issued menacing statements about witnesses in the case — from potentially interfering in the investigation.

Notably, Tennessee’s other U.S. senator, Marsha Blackburn, has sued Smith and the Justice Department in federal court, seeking an order that would require the government to destroy any remaining copies of her phone records. She is now the state’s Republican governor-elect.

The Board of Professional Responsibility of the Supreme Court of Tennessee and Hagerty did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Raskin makes formal ask for colleagues to support him as Judiciary chair
item.description: The Maryland Democrat is all but guaranteed the panel's top slot.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Jamie Raskin speaks with reporters as he departs a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 1, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, is officially asking his colleagues to support his bid to lead the panel in the majority as chair.

Raskin, in the letter obtained by POLITICO, lays out his vast investigative work in the minority ranging from exposing former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s conflicts of interest and work on the Jeffrey Epstein investigation. He also commits to “restore the rule of law and legislate against the disgraceful corruption of the government once we actually have the gavels.”

The Maryland Democrat and constitutional law professor vowed to “rein in ICE and its savage, lawless attacks” in the country, rebuild the Justice Department and FBI on principles of public integrity and impose a "$50 gift ban" on the Supreme Court. And he notes he will “extirpate bribery, kickbacks, inside dealing and sweetheart contracts in government.”

The letter is a formality, as Raskin is not expected to face any challengers and is widely revered across the caucus. He will, however, have to navigate some politically difficult territory once he takes the gavel, particularly whether to pursue impeachment proceedings against President Donald Trump or any number of his Cabinet officials.

Raskin said over the summer he would not rule it out.

item.title: House Republicans push for new rules targeting maverick holdouts
item.description: The disciplinary effort, sparked by the routine internal rebellions seen under Speaker Mike Johnson, could come to a head next week.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) applauds during a media availability after he was elected to be House Republican Leader for the upcoming 120th Congress on Capitol Hill on Nov. 10, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy and Meredith Lee Hill
item.dc:contributor: By Mia McCarthy and Meredith Lee Hill
item.content:encoded:
House Republicans are discussing whether to discipline members who vote against key GOP procedural motions or otherwise seek to undermine party leaders, according to six people granted anonymity to describe the behind-the-scenes effort.

The controversial fight is set to play out as the House GOP finalizes its conference rules package as soon as next week. If successful, it could begin to pull back power from maverick holdouts who successfully weaponized the thin Republican majority this Congress to elicit concessions from leadership.

They include members of the House Freedom Caucus, who frequently refused to advance GOP “rules” setting up floor debates, as well as Rep. Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, who used discharge petitions on multiple occasions to sidestep top party leaders. Many of those fractious members are considered allies of the incoming minority leader, Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan.

The debate is putting Jordan between scores of frustrated rank-and-file Republicans who want to see a crackdown and some of his hard-liner allies.

Rep. Mike Simpson (R-Idaho) said several House colleagues brought up the idea of punishing members during a closed-door GOP leadership election this week. Simpson said Friday he said he had “never” seen so many rebellions as Republicans saw in the past two years and said “a lot of members” want to prevent similar behavior in future GOP majorities.

“What do you do with those people?” Simpson said. “There's a lot of people that are very upset about that, and it's a hard thing to try to deal with. How do you punish them?”

Another House Republican granted anonymity to confirm the discussions said, “There’s a strong push for accountability for those who deliberately sabotage the will of the team.”

Luna said in an interview Friday she is opposed the move.

“There’s a difference between going against a rule and effectively preventing us from being able to legislate,” she said. “They’re effectively trying to control us.”

The conference rules debate was set to happen this week, but it was delayed indefinitely at Jordan’s behest after his election as GOP leader. It is expected to be rescheduled soon.

Simpson praised Jordan, saying he has been a “team player” since his failed speakership bid in 2023: “He always tried to convince the other people to vote for these rules,” he said. “He's been a good member, and I think that's exactly why he won.”

Any changes are likely to have negligible immediate effect as Republicans head deep into the minority, losing control of the floor. But some members are pushing the effort forward now to set a precedent for future GOP majorities and establish that Republicans cannot support Democratic procedural votes. Punishments could include stripping members of committee assignments or other actions, some of the people said.

Simpson said it may be “the perfect time” to act because “it probably really doesn’t matter right now.”

“We've been complaining about this for a long time," he said, while noting he himself had voted for a Democratic rule for a bill he’d negotiated, so “some leeway” would be appropriate.

item.title: Classified briefing set to include embattled Commerce official is postponed
item.description: Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees export controls and allegedly intervened on behalf of Nvidia, was to participate Tuesday in the session hosted by Commerce Chair Ted Cruz.

media:content.media:title: Jeffrey Kessler, nominee for undersecretary of Commerce for industry and security, testifies at a hearing of the Senate Banking Committee on Feb. 27, 2025, in Washington.

item.dc:creator: By Kelsey Brugger
item.content:encoded:
Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz has postponed a classified briefing that was scheduled for early next week and was set to include Jeffrey Kessler, the undersecretary of Commerce who has come under scrutiny this week for his dealings with chipmaker Nvidia.

In an email sent to committee members reviewed by POLITICO, the Texas Republican’s staff said the private briefing on recent cybersecurity breaches, including the hacking of Hugging Face by rogue OpenAI agents, would be delayed. The briefing would have also covered potential congressional action to address the growing threats posed by rapid advancements in artificial intelligence policy.

That Cruz intended to hold the briefing on Tuesday had not been previously reported.

“The topics will include: Mythos (pre-, during, and post-), federal government awareness of non-public loss-of-control events (Hugging Face incident), and potential congressional action for new authorities, among others,” the email read. Mythos is an advanced Anthropic model thought to be capable of breaching previously secure cyber systems.

The briefing was set as lawmakers grapple with how to coalesce around legislation that would enact federal standards on AI safety and establish oversight of the quickly developing technology. But efforts to strike a deal on AI safety fell apart before the November midterms and are expected to return in earnest in the new Congress when Democrats will control both chambers.

Kessler, the Commerce undersecretary for industry and security, has emerged as a potential key figure in the Nvidia meltdown after the global chipmaking superpower fired CEO Jensen Huang this week after his affair with a alleged Chinese spy surfaced.

The New York Times reported this week that Kessler intervened in an internal Commerce investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean firm led by the alleged Chinese spy that is a major buyer of advanced Nvidia chips. Kessler’s portfolio includes AI export controls.

A spokesperson for Cruz did not immediately respond to a request for comment nor did a Commerce Department spokesperson.

The other administration officials listed as expected to brief senators included Ethan Klein at the Office of Science and Technology Policy and Sean Cairncross, director of the Office of the National Cyber Director.

Asked by reporters Thursday about whether the panel would look into the Commerce Department’s role in the Nvidia story, Cruz said, “The Commerce Committee has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democratic presidents.”

item.title: Capitol agenda: Van Hollen's challenge puts Senate Dems in tough spot
item.description: Dozens of Democratic senators who have been lying low will now find it harder to hide.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen departs a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 12, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Senate Democrats just won a majority bigger than they even imagined. Now they’re going straight into a divisive leadership fight.

First, though, a thought for all the Democratic staff assistants who will be answering Senate office phones this month.

Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s announcement Thursday night, making his rumored challenge to longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer official, sets up an intense weekslong pressure campaign.

The dozens of Democratic senators who have been lying low, hoping to avoid a contested race as the party base clamors for new leadership, will now find it harder to hide.

Van Hollen made his calculation plain in an MS NOW interview after he made his announcement: “People will have to make a decision one way or the other.”

That threatens to publicly divide the caucus — and risks frustrating colleagues — at an otherwise triumphant moment. Senate Democrats began discussing their agenda for their first days in the majority this week in hopes of hitting the ground running in January. Now they are staring down weeks of attention on other matters.

Democrats are already discussing if they can short-circuit a drawn out leadership fight by moving up their leadership elections to next week, two people granted anonymity to disclose private talks.

Otherwise, the secret-ballot election will take place on Dec. 1.

The math as we know it still favors Schumer. Several have vowed publicly they will support him, and several more who were offered anonymity to avoid backlash have told POLITICO in recent weeks they back the incumbent leader as well.

Schumer said for the first time Thursday night, “I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” as Sens. Catherine Cortez Masto and Jacky Rosen of Nevada, and Angus King of Maine also made their support public.

Van Hollen acknowledged on MS NOW that he is the “underdog” in the race but said he had more than 10 commitments among the 55 Democrats who will vote (56 if Mary Peltola holds her lead in Alaska).

Two of the biggest names on the left — Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan — jumped behind Van Hollen after his announcement.

The Maryland senator, in so many words, pressed MS NOW viewers to burn up the Senate phone lines and pad his whip count.

“I think the American people want to see a little bit more democracy in the Senate Democratic Caucus,” he said.

What else we’re watching:

— DEMOCRATS PREP FOR SENIORITY SHOWDOWN: A fight is brewing among House Democrats over the tenure-based system for committee leadership roles. Rep. Janelle Bynum (D-Ore.) is pitching that “subcommittee leaders be chosen based on merit, not seniority alone.” That could be seen as an incremental alternative to a more controversial proposal from Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.) that would impose a four-term limit on full committee chairs.

— MORAN VS. MURKOWSKI: Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) says he’s “pursuing” a bid for the top GOP spot on the Senate Appropriations Committee — leapfrogging more senior Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska). He has until early January to decide whether he’ll force a vote among Republican appropriators, after which the full GOP conference will need to decide whether to accept that choice or tell members of the committee to pick someone else.

Jordain Carney, Riley Rogerson and Jennifer Scholtes contributed to this report.

item.title: Tim Kaine to chair Senate Budget Committee next year
item.description: The Virginia Democrat has served on the panel for almost 14 years.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) speaks with reporters about President Donald Trump's foreign policy intentions, with Venezuela in particular, at the Capitol in Washington, Thursday, Nov. 6, 2025.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes and Jordain Carney
item.dc:contributor: By Jennifer Scholtes and Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Tim Kaine confirmed Thursday that he will chair the Senate Budget Committee next year, touting the power of the party-line reconciliation process to “provide relief to everyday Americans.”

The Virginia Democrat, who has served on the panel for almost 14 years, said lawmakers need to reverse cuts to Medicaid and nutrition assistance and “stop funding illegal and foolish wars,” while investing in education, housing, workforce training, health care and infrastructure.

Citing his time as mayor of Richmond and governor of Virginia during the fiscal crisis that began in 2008, Kaine vowed bold action to prevent automatic cuts to Social Security benefits in the coming years and manage the rising national debt.

item.title: Chris Van Hollen says he will run for Senate majority leader
item.description: The announcement is a setback for longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who remains favored to win.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) speaks with reporters as he boards a vehicle to depart a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 12, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen said Thursday that he will run for majority leader, challenging longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer.

Van Hollen said in a statement that the midterm election results are a sign Americans want “change” not only from “Donald Trump’s disastrous policies” but also from a “status quo that isn’t working for working people.”

“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people,” he said in the statement.

Van Hollen’s decision is a setback to Schumer, who remains favored to become leader buthad previously predicted that he would not have a challenge. Democrats will hold their caucus elections next month.

Schumer has repeatedly predicted since the Democrats won a majority in last week’s midterms that he will be elected majority leader. In a statement after Van Hollen’s announcement Thursday, he said he has already locked up the votes in the race.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said in a social media post.

“I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” he added.

Van Hollen said in an MSNOW interview he had the support of more than 10 of the 55 Democratic senators who are known to be voting but acknowledged that he was the “underdog” in the race.

“I've gotten feedback from members of the caucus,” Van Hollen added. “And my view is this is very much in flux. … People will have to make a decision one way or the other.”

Several Senate Democrats — including Ruben Gallego of Arizona, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and Kirsten Gillibrand of New York — have publicly said they will support Schumer for leader. Several other Democratic senators who were granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive leadership race have said either in interviews or through their offices that they intend to vote for Schumer during the closed-door election.

Sen. Angus King (I-Maine), who caucuses with Democrats, said in a statement Thursday night that he is backing Schumer for leader, calling him “one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history.”

But Schumer, 75, has emerged as a frequent target for the party’s base, which began calling for his ouster last year after he helped advance a GOP funding bill to avert a shutdown just a couple of months into Donald Trump’s second term.

Even as Schumer has worked to try to shore up his standing within the caucus since then, progressives in his party haven’t forgiven him, and a crop of incoming senators — including Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Troy Jackson of Maine — have said they do not plan to support him.

El-Sayed and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said publicly Thursday they would back Van Hollen.

It’s the culmination of a two-year transformation of a longtime fixture of the Democratic establishment. Van Hollen, 67, has held public office continuously since 1991 — spending 14 years in the House, some of it in leadership, before being elected to the Senate in 2016.

But Van Hollen has grownmore critical of party leaders in recent years, particularly their approach to President Donald Trump and the U.S.-Israel relationship. He jumped into the national spotlight last year when he became the first U.S. lawmaker to visit the El Salvador prison where the administration was sending scores of deportees — including a Maryland man, Kilmar Ábrego García, who had been mistakenly deported in contravention of a court order.

He said earlier this year that he was eyeing a 2028 presidential bid as some Democrats privately speculated last month that a senator with higher ambitions might challenge Schumer in a profile-raising bid.

Van Hollen’s thinking on the leadership race evolved after Democrats’ sweeping election win, a grassroots push for change atop the caucus and a flood of supportive calls, a Senate aide granted anonymity to describe his thinking previously told POLITICO.

Van Hollen told reporters this week that he didn’t believe Schumer should have a “coronation.”

“We should not support anybody for leader without a very clear plan,” he said, “and as you know, there are many people who think that a change is required.”

item.title: Democrats eye spring government funding punt
item.description: The party still needs to land on a strategy to curtail Iran war funding in the coming weeks.

media:content.media:title: Jeffries said Thursday that Democrats "will continue to do everything we can to end" the war in Iran.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney, Jennifer Scholtes and Riley Rogerson
item.dc:contributor: By Jordain Carney, Jennifer Scholtes and Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Top congressional Democrats are looking to avoid a spending confrontation with President Donald Trump and Republicans in the early months of their new majorities.

Two people granted anonymity to describe private strategy said the Democrats are discussing seeking a punt that would go into March or April as they negotiate a stopgap funding bill ahead of an upcoming Dec. 11 deadline.

A showdown is still possible next month, however, over Iran war funding. While Republicans remain in charge, Democratic leaders are under intense pressure to use their spending powers to end hostilities — potentially sparking a government shutdown.

Some members in both the House and Senate are already pushing to include language in the expected stopgap bill to block any funding for the conflict. Key leaders have also said they want to end the war but have yet specified their demands ahead of the December deadline.

But Democrats otherwise want to spend their early days in power focused on executing an affordability policy agenda without getting mired in shutdown threats or brinkmanship with Trump.

Senate Democrats talked during a closed-door lunch this week about potential options for what Iran-related language in a December stopgap could look like. Meanwhile, Republicans have sought to continue business as usual, releasing new fiscal 2027 funding bills even as they acknowledge the need for a funding punt next month.

Conversations over the stopgap are still preliminary, and Democrats will need to work out a deal with Republicans on both the date and any Iran language.

“We are exploring every option to figure out how to end the war in Iran,” Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democratic appropriator in the Senate, said in an interview earlier this week. “I don't trust [Trump] at all. So we are looking [at] what language we can put in here that will actually make sure that we are writing bills that the American people voted for.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is expected to be speaker next year, told reporters Thursday that House Democrats have been “strongly opposed to this war from Day 1, and we will continue to do everything we can to end it.”

He said Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top House Democratic appropriator, would evaluate how to deal with war funding.

“She’s working through all of our Democratic priorities to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11,” Jeffries added.

DeLauro told reporters this week that she still wants a stopgap that is “as short as possible.”

item.title: Democrats eye restoring proxy voting in the House — with limits
item.description: The pandemic-era policy allowing members to vote remotely in a wide variety of circumstances is unlikely to fully return.

media:content.media:title: Reps. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) and Brittany Pettersen (D-Colo.) teamed up last year to promote proxy voting for new parents.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
House Democrats are moving toward allowing members to vote on the floor by proxy again after Republicans ended the Covid-era practice in 2023 — but the free-for-all rules that resulted in scores of members routinely voting remotely are unlikely to return.

Instead, members are coalescing around narrower proposals that would allow only new parents or those undergoing medical treatment to have colleagues cast their votes.

“We want to be responsive to members and their growing families, and be helpful to that, while understanding the complexities of actually voting here in this body,” Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, House Democrats’ No. 3, said in an interview.

Proxy voting is one of the many items House Democrats are weighing for inclusion in the rules governing the chamber in the next Congress. When Republicans took over the last time the majority changed hands in 2023, ending the practice was one of their top priorities. The then-incoming speaker, Kevin McCarthy, had unsuccessfully sued to block it as unconstitutional.

The practice was instituted in 2020 under then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi in the depths of the pandemic and it was used by hundreds of members of both parties in the nearly three years it was in effect. But now Democrats say they are cool to fully resurrecting what had been billed as an emergency measure.

“It's important that we're here,” Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Ill.), who underwent foot surgery this year and got a doctor’s permission to return to Capitol Hill early to avoid missing votes. “I recognize I want to welcome people who are in different stages in life, and that includes young people who may be starting a family. … So you have to figure out exactly how it would be set up in a way that it's not abused.”

Rep. Brittany Pettersen (D-Colo.) led a bipartisan effort last year that would have allowed 12 weeks of remote voting for new parents. She said in an interview that she has proposed that the same policy be included in the upcoming House rules package, with the addition of parents who are adopting.

“I'm grateful that leadership has been open and supportive of the idea,” she said in an interview. “We're going to work through that process, and I'm hopeful that we'll actually change the rules so that this place is more accessible to parents.”

Her 2025 bill has 175 co-sponsors, including nine Republicans. Hakeem Jeffries, the presumptive incoming speaker, endorsed new-parent proxy voting at a Thursday news conference.

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) tried to force Republican leaders to take up the policy last year, filing a discharge petition to send the issue straight to the floor only to scuttle the effort after a protracted battle with Speaker Mike Johnson. Luna said she has spoken to Democrats, including fellow Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz, about advancing the policy next term and said in an interview, “I don't see why they wouldn't do that.”

“People talk about wanting Congress to get younger,” Moskowitz said in an interview. “Younger people are going to come with young kids and families, and so ultimately I do think for maternity and paternity leave we should look at that — for a limited period of time.”

Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.) said she was confident the new-parent provision would be included and said “the question is what else gets included beyond parental leave.”

One idea floating around the caucus is to allow proxy voting for members on health leave or otherwise institute a policy that would allow leadership to review proxy voting requests on a case-by-case basis.

Rep. Linda Sanchez (D-Calif.) previously backed an effort to codify sick leave proxy voting and said she would support including it in the new rules. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who battled cancer last term, said “the devil is in the details with that, but I've been open to where there's some kind of compelling medical necessity.”

But in terms of resurrecting the pandemic-era approach, which saw many members voting by proxy while they attended campaign and personal events, many Democrats aren’t interested in going back.

“It was getting out of hand there at the end during Covid, when people weren't using it for Covid,” Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) said in an interview. “I think it makes more sense to carve out limited exceptions.”

Mia McCarthy contributed to this report.

item.title: Moran 'pursuing' challenge to Murkowski for powerful appropriations perch
item.description: The Kansas Republican said GOP senators will need to decide.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on June 4, 2025.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes and Jordain Carney
item.dc:contributor: By Jennifer Scholtes and Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Two Republicans are set to face off for the top GOP spot on the Senate Appropriations Committee in the coming weeks, with Kansas Sen. Jerry Moran saying he'll challenge Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski for the seat.

“I'm still pursuing that opportunity,” Moran said in an interview Thursday afternoon.

Murkowski is next in line for the role under the Senate Republican Conference's seniority policy, and her office confirmed this week that she intends to seek the position following the election defeat of the current chair, Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, in last week's midterms.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said in a brief interview Thursday that he is currently staying out of the dispute. “I haven't weighed into that,” he said, adding that he told Murkowski that she and Moran “need to talk it out” and that “we’ll see where those conversations lead."

But Moran said the two have already discussed the issue, and neither is budging. “She and I have been talking on several occasions since this began,” he said. “But I'm not sure how you talk this to a conclusion.”

Moran said GOP senators on the Appropriations Committee will first weigh in, followed by a vote by all Senate Republicans. While it’s possible internal conference decisions could be made this year, the Senate is set to ratify those selections on the floor in early January.

Moran would not say whether he would stop pursuing his party's top committee spot if he were promised a choice subcommittee perch like leading the defense funding panel. But he said Murkowski intends to take the top Republican spot on both the full committee and the coveted subcommittee in charge of doling out roughly $1 trillion for military programs each year.

Asked about Moran’s challenge, Murkowski said Thursday that she would “rather talk with members than talk through the press,” adding, “I think that's how we respect one another.”
